title: Kassapa's mountains
hookLine: the old ascetic loves the rocky hills, the rain, the elephants (Theragatha, Mahakassapa)

cards: Rocky slopes. Clear, cool water. Elephants trumpeting somewhere below.

It could be a postcard, but it's a run of pictures from the verses the Theragatha gives to Mahakassapa, the stern elder met earlier this year, whom tradition remembers for the strict practices: rag robes, plain food, the forest.
Today he does something softer. In his own song, he tells you what he loves.

teach.h: THE REFRAIN: THOSE HILLS DELIGHT ME.
teach.b: First, the refrain. After each picture of the hills, Kassapa says the same thing: those rocky hills delight me. Again, and again.
The elder known for doing without is, in his own words, full of delight. Second, what's in the hills.

teach.h: WATER, ELEPHANTS, RAIN, ROOM TO SIT.
teach.b: Streams of clear, cool water. Slopes where elephants pass. The calls of birds.
Rain on the rock. Room to sit alone. Nothing on that list is a luxury, and none of it belongs to him.
His verses open by warning against going about surrounded by a crowd, where the mind gets pulled this way and that. The hills are the other side of that warning: where he can practice.
So the delight isn't instead of the discipline. It grows right out of it. Fourth, the kind of joy it is.
Not the joy of owning a view. Kassapa doesn't speak of owning anything up there. He comes, he sits, the rain falls, he goes down for alms and comes back.

Some readers are surprised that a man of strict habits sings about beauty at all. The poem doesn't seem to feel any tension in it. A hard life can still have a place it loves, and say so without embarrassment.
These hills delight me isn't a confession. It's simple news from the ridge.

how: Forest monasteries in the Theravada tradition are often set in hills and woods, and teachers read Mahakassapa's verses as a picture of how simple living and delight in nature go together.

o: the rocky hills the stern elder Kassapa loved
a far hill where monks were sent as a penalty
the mountain where the Buddha first taught

p: the stern elder who loved the hills

s: Kassapa's song is all about doing without
his refrain is delight: those rocky hills delight me.
his verses warn against going about surrounded by a crowd
the hills are the other side of that warning: room to practice.
Kassapa's hills are empty of animals
elephants pass on the slopes, and birds call.

games.q: you're Mahakassapa, an old monk known for keeping the strict practices. someone asks if there's anything you love. what do you say?
o: the crowds who come to hear me.
games.why: his own verses repeat it again and again: those rocky hills delight me. delight and discipline sit together in his song.

practice: Find a hill outside your window, or bring one to mind, a slope you climbed as a kid, a ridge from a trip, the mound in a park, and see its shape: the rock, the grass, the sky behind it.
Let the breath slow to the pace of something that doesn't move. When the mind wanders, come back to the hill; it hasn't gone anywhere.

wordCard.voice: Kassapa's mountains. The rocky hills the stern elder sang about: cool water, rain, elephants, room to sit alone, and his refrain that they delight him. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali: sela, rock, a rocky hill. The hills of Kassapa's refrain.

carryVoice: Your line: these hills delight me. A strict life and a glad heart sat on the same ridge. See you tomorrow.
